replies.author: Some_Safe_300
replies.body:
Here's Fable's explanation, my prompts for the music were pretty simple:

The music is generated live in the browser — there are no audio files at all. Everything is synthesized from scratch using the Web Audio API (oscillators, noise, and filters), in Music.ts.

In simple terms:

Every instrument is fake, built from basic waveforms. A "flute" is a sine wave with vibrato and a bit of noise for breath; a "lute" is a pluck whose brightness fades quickly like a real string; drums are pitch-dropping sine thumps plus filtered noise. Small tricks (a strum stagger, a tin whistle "scooping" up into its note) make them read as real instruments.

The score has three moods, picked by what you're doing:

Exploration — slow, pastoral D-major music (pads, harp arpeggios, occasional flute/horn melodies). It's generative: chord progressions and melody phrases are semi-randomly assembled, and like WoW zone music it plays a "piece" for a while, then rests in silence before starting a new one.

Combat — fast D-minor with taiko drums, snare, and brass stabs, kicking in when you enter a fight and lingering a moment after it ends.

Inn — the one hand-written tune: a 32-bar 6/8 tavern melody in G major, played by a "band" that grows section by section (whistle and lute first, then fiddle and drum, then everyone). It's written out rather than generated so it's actually hummable.

Timing works by scheduling ahead. A timer fires every 120 ms and schedules whole bars of notes about half a second before they play, so the audio stays smooth even if a frame hiccups. Mood changes crossfade between three mixer buses rather than stopping and starting.

Sound effects and ambience elsewhere in src/client/audio/ are synthesized the same way.

replies.author: ElwinLewis
replies.body:
Vibecoders rejoice 

Assuming **VAT = Vertex Animation Textures**: **yes, today’s frontier models can build both multithreading and VAT into a Three.js application.** The Reddit comment is fair as criticism of *unspecified, one-shot vibe coding*—not as a statement about what the models are capable of.  
**Multithreading**  
A model can architect:  
A main UI thread plus Web Workers for physics, procedural geometry, pathfinding, simulation, decompression, and world generation.  
Transferable ArrayBuffers to avoid copying large geometry data.  
SharedArrayBuffer and Atomics for shared-state workloads, provided the server has the required cross-origin-isolation headers.  
Rendering inside a worker using OffscreenCanvas, although DOM interaction must remain outside the worker.  
These are standard browser capabilities: workers execute JavaScript on background threads, and current Three.js supports OffscreenCanvas as a renderer canvas. Shared memory has additional security and deployment requirements.   
But “multithread the Three.js app” is not a sufficient instruction. The model needs to determine:  
What is actually CPU-bound.  
Whether messaging overhead exceeds the saved work.  
Who owns each buffer.  
How state synchronization works.  
Whether rendering should move off-thread or only simulation should.  
The usual sensible design is **one render thread plus one or more workload-specific workers**, not blindly splitting every system across threads.  
**VAT**  
VAT is arguably easier for a strong model because the runtime concept is straightforward:  
Bake each vertex’s positions—and sometimes normals, rotations or pivots—into textures.  
Give each vertex an address into those textures.  
Sample the appropriate frame in a vertex shader.  
Interpolate frames and optionally vary playback per instance.  
VAT shifts deformation work onto the GPU and is particularly useful for complex animations and large numbers of instanced animated meshes.   
A frontier model can write:  
The Three.js ShaderMaterial, TSL or WGSL implementation.  
Frame interpolation and animation controls.  
Instanced per-object playback offsets.  
Texture-loading and validation code.  
Houdini or Blender export tooling.  
WebGL2 and WebGPU variants.  
The difficult part is not generating shader syntax. It is correctly matching the shader to the **baking convention**: texture dimensions, vertex ordering, bounding-box decoding, pivot handling, normal encoding, precision, coordinate systems and exported metadata. Give the model the actual VAT files and export settings, and it has a strong chance. Tell it only “add VAT,” and hallucinated assumptions are likely.  
**What frontier models change**  
Current coding agents are no longer limited to producing isolated snippets. The strongest models can inspect repositories, run builds and tests, operate browsers, examine rendered output, profile failures and revise implementations over long sessions. OpenAI reports state-of-the-art coding-agent results for GPT-5.6 and specifically highlights complex frontend and game-building workflows; public coding-evaluation performance has also risen sharply, although benchmark scores still do not equal guaranteed production reliability.
